name: Chalon
catalog_citation: DerSimonian, Nicole. 2015. Sketch of Chalon Phonology. MA thesis (Linguistics), California State University, Fresno. vii+49 pp. (57 pp. PDF; committee: Chris Golston (chair), Sean Fulop, Brian Agbayani).
catalog_locator: Chapter 2 'Sketch of Chalon Phonology', section 'Stress' > 'Primary Stress Rule', thesis pp. 13-14 (section 'Stress' begins p. 12; exceptions under 'Morphology' pp. 15-17; Appendix D 'Stressed words' pp. 38ff.)
catalog_quote: The majority of the data present in Henshaw show stress in Chalon to be a Quantity Insensitive Trochaic system. Examples of the primary stress pattern are demonstrated in (15), where polysyllabic words have trochees with primary stress, and all feet to the left. [...] Patterns of stress on heavy and light syllables are variable; primary stress placement is not dependent on syllable weight. Instead, words in Chalon are shown to be quantity insensitive, and seem to follow an initial, trochaic stress rule, which is further examined in the following section. [...] The data from Henshaw show that of the 214 words transcribed with stress, 73% follow this trochaic pattern.

Identity: Ch. 1 (thesis p. 1) 'Chalon is a Costanoan language that is part of the Utian language family in California. The oldest text was written between 1829-1835 by father Vicente Sarria of Mission Soledad'; data = Henshaw (1955) and Pinart (1952) Soledad vocabularies…
new_statements.relation_note: States an initial, quantity-insensitive trochaic primary-stress rule for Chalon (73% of Henshaw's 214 stress-marked words), with morphologically conditioned exceptions; no tone. Also gives consonant/vowel inventories, geminates, diphthongs, long vowels, syllable structure, [h]~[x] complementary distribution.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the word-initial syllable: a single quantity-insensitive trochee aligned at the left edge (OT: TROCHEE, ALL-FT-L); syllable weight plays no role. Established philologically from Henshaw's accent marks (214 stress-marked words, 73% initial).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not established: 'words that appear to have two stresses like 19g [(ˈhit.sa)(ˈko.ro) 'foot'] could be demonstrating secondary stress, or could be the result of compounding. Still, the data are inconclusive' (p. 17).
new_statements.exceptions: 58 of 214 stress-marked words deviate (stress on peninitial, antepenult, penult or final syllable, ex. (19) pp. 15-16); attributed partly to morphology: possessive prefixes such as ik- 'my' are never stressed and stress then falls on the stem-initial syllable; deictic proclitics nɛppɪ-/nuppɪ- 'this/that' are variably stressed (ex. 20); some marks may be transcriber inaccuracies. Also notes (p. 12-13) that Henshaw is the only Chalon source marking stress (56% of his 380 words), mostly on single words, with sparse phrase-level marking.
new_statements.identity_note: Explicitly Chalon of Mission Soledad (Southern Costanoan, with Mutsun and Rumsen as the named sister languages); data are Henshaw's 1884 Soledad schedule (Heizer 1955) and Pinart's 1878 Soledad vocabulary (Heizer 1952), i.e. exactly the chal1270 corpus. Not a namesake.

sources.note: Costanoan section (pp. 239-242) treats Soledad only as one of seven mission dialects, with 'the scant 22 words known from Soledad' (Hale via Gallatin 1848, p. 241); no phonetic, accent or stress statement for Soledad/Chalon.

sources.citation: Hale, Horatio. 1846. Ethnography and Philology. United States Exploring Expedition vol. VI. Philadelphia: C. Sherman. (CIHM microform scan, archive.org cihm_35669)
sources.note: pp. 633-634: a short 'La Soledad' wordlist ('The few words which were obtained will serve at least to..'), the only Chalon data; the general orthography note in the front matter (par. 5) says the acute accent marks 'those syllables on which the stress of voice falls' - a transcription convention for the whole volume, not a statement about Chalon stress placement. scanned of the list is poor.

sources.citation: [Ryan, Mark (transcriber/editor), with Chris Golston]. 2016. English-Chalon / Chalon-English Dictionary. 'From the glossary of David Leedom Shaul, Department of Anthropology, University of Wyoming, which was compiled from the texts of H. W. Henshaw, Alphonse Pinart, and Fr. Vincente Sarria'; with introductory notes on the Chalon Alphabet by Chris Golston (Indigenous Language Group, California State University Fresno). Chalon Council of Bakersfield (posted online 2017), 44 pp.
sources.note: Golston's 'Chalon Alphabet' notes (pp. 2-3) cover only segments and length: consonant chart (p t d c-hacek k glottal stop; s s-hacek x h; m n; w l r y), vowels a e i o u 'pronounced like those of Spanish', geminate consonants and double vowels 'sound just like single.. but last longer', dental vs alveolar t/d, x 'like a really rough h', and the remark that x and h may be one phoneme in complementary distribution '(Dersimonian 2014)'. There is no sentence about stress, accent or syllable prominence, and none about tone. About 100 dictionary entries nevertheless carry an acute accent inherited…

sources.citation: Levy, Richard L. 1976. Costanoan Internal Relationships. (Publications of the University of California Archaeological Research Facility, non-serial.) Berkeley: Archaeological Research Facility, Department of Anthropology, University of California. 57 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 3.0 'Phonological Systems' (pp. 4-5) is the only synchronic phonology: 'It is fortunate that the Costanoan languages had a relatively simple phonological system. All eight languages had a simple five vowel system and phonemic vowel length.. Only Pinart and Harrington recorded vowel length and geminate consonants.. /h/ is restricted to initial position in those languages in which it occurs but is not always distinguished from /x/.' and, for this languoid: 'Awaswas and Chalon are problematical. They almost certainly lacked /c[retroflex]/, which is extremely rare in both languages in which…

sources.citation: Heizer, R. F. (ed.) 1955. California Indian Linguistic Records: The Mission Indian Vocabularies of H. W. Henshaw. Anthropological Records 15(2):85-202.
sources.note: Henshaw's BAE-schedule Soledad (Chalon) vocabulary; BAE schedules routinely mark stressed syllables, so the list may show stress placement word by word.

sources.citation: Heizer, R. F. (ed.) 1952. California Indian Linguistic Records: The Mission Indian Vocabularies of Alphonse Pinart. Anthropological Records 15(1):1-84.
sources.note: Largest Chalon (Costanoan I, Soledad) vocabulary; Pinart's transcription may mark accent on individual words and Heizer's editorial introduction may comment on his accent notation - the only route to an empirical stress pattern for Chalon.

sources.citation: Kroeber, A. L. 1904. The Languages of the Coast of California South of San Francisco. UCPAAE 2(2):29-80 (in the whole-volume scan of UCPAAE vol. 2).
sources.note: Costanoan chapter (pp. 69ff.) and its Phonetics section describe Rumsien (Carmel/Monterey) from three informants; Soledad/Chalon is not treated at all (the only 'Soledad' hit in the volume is a place-name gloss).
